claim: Shigella flexneri is the most common cause of bacterial dysentery in low-income countries.
source: Shigella flexneri is the most common cause of bacterial dysentery in low-income countries.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract without supporting data in the manuscript itself, but is presented as established knowledge.

claim: S. flexneri is subdivided into seven phylogenetic groups (PGs).
source: Our analysis subdivides S. flexneri into seven phylogenetic groups (PGs); each containing two-or-more serotypes and characterised by distinct virulence gene complement and geographic range.
evidence: This claim is supported by BAPS clustering analysis and phylogenetic reconstruction shown in Figure 1.

claim: Each phylogenetic group contains two or more serotypes.
source: Our analysis subdivides S. flexneri into seven phylogenetic groups (PGs); each containing two-or-more serotypes and characterised by distinct virulence gene complement and geographic range.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the serotype composition shown in Figure 1 pie charts.

claim: Each phylogenetic group is characterized by distinct virulence gene complement.
source: Our analysis subdivides S. flexneri into seven phylogenetic groups (PGs); each containing two-or-more serotypes and characterised by distinct virulence gene complement and geographic range.
evidence: This is supported by the virulence gene distribution analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Each phylogenetic group is characterized by distinct geographic range.
source: Our analysis subdivides S. flexneri into seven phylogenetic groups (PGs); each containing two-or-more serotypes and characterised by distinct virulence gene complement and geographic range.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the geographic composition shown in Figure 1 pie charts and phylogeographic analyses in Figure 1 supplements 4-7.

claim: Geographically restricted sub-lineages of S. flexneri have persistently colonized regions for many decades to over 100 years.
source: Within the S. flexneri PGs we identify geographically restricted sub-lineages that appear to have persistently colonised regions for many decades to over 100 years.
evidence: This is supported by BEAST temporal analysis showing MRCA dates and geographic clustering patterns in Figure 1 supplements 4-7.

claim: There is abundant evidence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) determinant acquisition in S. flexneri.
source: Although we found abundant evidence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) determinant acquisition, our dataset shows no evidence of subsequent intercontinental spread of antimicrobial resistant strains.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the AMR gene distribution shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3.

claim: There is no evidence of intercontinental spread of antimicrobial resistant S. flexneri strains.
source: Although we found abundant evidence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) determinant acquisition, our dataset shows no evidence of subsequent intercontinental spread of antimicrobial resistant strains.
evidence: This is supported by the phylogeographic analysis showing geographic restriction of AMR-carrying lineages in Figure 2 and Figure 2 supplement 3.

claim: The pattern of colonization and AMR gene acquisition suggest that S. flexneri has a distinct life-cycle involving local persistence.
source: The pattern of colonisation and AMR gene acquisition suggest that S. flexneri has a distinct life-cycle involving local persistence.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogeographic patterns and AMR distribution data presented in Figures 1-3.

claim: Shigella spp. cause approximately 165 million new infections globally per year.
source: The 'genus' Shigella consists of four species (Shigella flexneri, Shigella sonnei, Shigella boydii and Shigella dysenteriae) causes approximately 165 million new infections globally per year (Kotloff et al., 1999; Ram et al., 2008), which have previously been estimated to result in up to 1 million deaths annually (Kotloff et al., 1999, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Shigella infections have previously been estimated to result in up to 1 million deaths annually.
source: The 'genus' Shigella consists of four species (Shigella flexneri, Shigella sonnei, Shigella boydii and Shigella dysenteriae) causes approximately 165 million new infections globally per year (Kotloff et al., 1999; Ram et al., 2008), which have previously been estimated to result in up to 1 million deaths annually (Kotloff et al., 1999, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The vast majority of Shigella cases and fatalities occur in low to middle-income countries in children under the age of 5 years.
source: The vast majority of cases and fatalities occur in low to middle-income countries in children under the age of 5 years (Kotloff et al., 1999; von Seidlein et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The preponderance of Shigella cases are attributable to endemic disease caused by S. flexneri.
source: The preponderance of these cases are attributable to endemic disease caused by the species S. flexneri (Vinh et al., 2009; Ud-Din et al., 2013; Livio et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Many genes that determine serotype in S. flexneri are encoded on horizontally transmissible genetic elements.
source: Although serotyping still forms the central vocabulary for describing this species it is now widely agreed that many genes that determine serotype are encoded on horizontally transmissible genetic elements (Allison and Verma, 2000), thus facilitating serotype switching.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Shigella spp. represent distinct clades that fall within the E. coli species complex.
source: Through limited genetic and genomic studies we know that Shigella spp. represent distinct clades that fall within the E. coli species complex (Pupo et al., 2000; Yang et al., 2005, 2007; Ashton et al., 2014; Sahl et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: There are two distinct S. flexneri lineages.
source: These studies show the existence of two distinct S. flexneri lineages, with one lineage including only a single serotype (S. flexneri 6) (Choi et al., 2007) that clusters within species S. boydii (Yang et al., 2007) and possesses a different LPS O-antigen.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: One S. flexneri lineage includes only serotype 6, clusters within S. boydii, and possesses a different LPS O-antigen.
source: These studies show the existence of two distinct S. flexneri lineages, with one lineage including only a single serotype (S. flexneri 6) (Choi et al., 2007) that clusters within species S. boydii (Yang et al., 2007) and possesses a different LPS O-antigen.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The second monophyletic S. flexneri group contains representatives of all other S. flexneri serotypes (1–5, X, Y) and is responsible for the majority of S. flexneri disease.
source: The second monophyletic S. flexneri group contains representatives of all other S. flexneri serotypes (1–5, X, Y) and is responsible for the majority of S. flexneri disease; it is this main lineage that is examined here.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature and defines the scope of the study.

claim: S. dysenteriae type 1 is an epidemic pathogen characterized by sporadic, large scale outbreaks that spread rapidly and widely via intercontinental transmissions.
source: Work on the now rarely isolated (von Seidlein et al., 2006), S. dysenteriae type 1 has shown it to be an epidemic pathogen characterised by sporadic, large scale outbreaks that spread rapidly and widely via a series of intercontinental transmissions, often associated with war or famine (Rohmer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: S. sonnei is highly clonal.
source: Studies examining the dominant endemic Shigella species of industrialised and newly industrialised countries, S. sonnei, have also revealed a species that is highly clonal (Karaolis et al., 1994; Holt et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: S. sonnei evolved in Europe approximately 300 years ago.
source: S. sonnei evolved in Europe ∼300 years ago and has recently moved out of this region via intercontinental spread as a single, rapidly evolving lineage, establishing new, local, populations in countries as they industrialise (Holt et al., 2012, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: S. sonnei has recently moved out of Europe via intercontinental spread as a single, rapidly evolving lineage.
source: S. sonnei evolved in Europe ∼300 years ago and has recently moved out of this region via intercontinental spread as a single, rapidly evolving lineage, establishing new, local, populations in countries as they industrialise (Holt et al., 2012, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: S. flexneri accounts for over 50% of all cases of shigellosis in multiple studies.
source: S. flexneri remains the dominant species in low-income countries (multiple studies report over 50% of all cases of shigellosis [Kotloff et al., 1999, 2013; Livio et al., 2014]), whereas S. sonnei is the most commonly isolated Shigella species in industrialised countries (77% of cases as reported by Kotloff et al., 1999) where there is better sanitation and access to clean food and drinking water.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: S. sonnei accounts for 77% of Shigella cases in industrialized countries.
source: S. flexneri remains the dominant species in low-income countries (multiple studies report over 50% of all cases of shigellosis [Kotloff et al., 1999, 2013; Livio et al., 2014]), whereas S. sonnei is the most commonly isolated Shigella species in industrialised countries (77% of cases as reported by Kotloff et al., 1999) where there is better sanitation and access to clean food and drinking water.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The study gathered a representative global collection of 351 isolates of S. flexneri spanning serotypes 1–5, X, Xv and Y.
source: To further our understanding of the evolution, population structure and phylogeography of S. flexneri we gathered a representative global collection of 351 isolates of S. flexneri, spanning serotypes 1–5, X, Xv and Y, collected from the contemporary principal foci of endemic disease; Africa, Asia and South and Central America as well as historical isolates from reference collections dating back to 1914 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the study design and sample collection.

claim: The S. flexneri isolates were collected from Africa, Asia, South and Central America, and include historical isolates dating back to 1914.
source: To further our understanding of the evolution, population structure and phylogeography of S. flexneri we gathered a representative global collection of 351 isolates of S. flexneri, spanning serotypes 1–5, X, Xv and Y, collected from the contemporary principal foci of endemic disease; Africa, Asia and South and Central America as well as historical isolates from reference collections dating back to 1914 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the study design and sample collection.

claim: 67,981 SNPs were identified among the 352 genomes (including reference genome).
source: We identified 67,981 SNPs among the 352 genomes (including reference genome), with 63,186 of these on the chromosome and 4795 on the VP.
evidence: This is a direct result from the SNP calling analysis.

claim: 63,186 SNPs were identified on the chromosome.
source: We identified 67,981 SNPs among the 352 genomes (including reference genome), with 63,186 of these on the chromosome and 4795 on the VP.
evidence: This is a direct result from the SNP calling analysis.

claim: 4,795 SNPs were identified on the virulence plasmid.
source: We identified 67,981 SNPs among the 352 genomes (including reference genome), with 63,186 of these on the chromosome and 4795 on the VP.
evidence: This is a direct result from the SNP calling analysis.

claim: After removal of recombinant regions, 55,662 SNPs remained in total.
source: Following the removal of recombinant regions (almost entirely concentrated in phage, IS elements and S. flexneri Pathogenic Islands, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), 55,662 SNPs remained in total, with 53,078 on the chromosome and 2584 on the VP.
evidence: This is a direct result from the recombination filtering analysis.

claim: After removal of recombinant regions, 53,078 SNPs remained on the chromosome.
source: Following the removal of recombinant regions (almost entirely concentrated in phage, IS elements and S. flexneri Pathogenic Islands, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), 55,662 SNPs remained in total, with 53,078 on the chromosome and 2584 on the VP.
evidence: This is a direct result from the recombination filtering analysis.

claim: After removal of recombinant regions, 2,584 SNPs remained on the virulence plasmid.
source: Following the removal of recombinant regions (almost entirely concentrated in phage, IS elements and S. flexneri Pathogenic Islands, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), 55,662 SNPs remained in total, with 53,078 on the chromosome and 2584 on the VP.
evidence: This is a direct result from the recombination filtering analysis.

claim: Recombinant regions were almost entirely concentrated in phage, IS elements and S. flexneri Pathogenic Islands.
source: Following the removal of recombinant regions (almost entirely concentrated in phage, IS elements and S. flexneri Pathogenic Islands, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), 55,662 SNPs remained in total, with 53,078 on the chromosome and 2584 on the VP.
evidence: This is supported by the recombination analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The virulence plasmid phylogeny precisely mirrors that of the chromosome, indicating co-evolution.
source: Performing the BAPS analysis on alignments of the chromosome and VP collectively or individually resulted in the same pattern of clustering, reflecting that the VP phylogeny precisely mirrors that of the chromosome, indicating co-evolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the congruent phylogenies shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The phylogenetic groups are separated by considerable evolutionary distance, ranging from 1138 to 8430 SNPs between PGs.
source: Genetic clustering of the population and the phylogenetic tree revealed a species that is composed of seven discrete PGs, separated by considerable evolutionary distance (ranging from 1138 to 8430 SNPs between PGs—Figure 1—figure supplement 2), this analysis provided only limited information regarding the natural history of the organism.
evidence: This is shown in the table in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mutation rates among phylogenetic groups were similar, ranging between 6.46 × 10−7 and 9.54 × 10−7 substitutions per site per year.
source: Inferring evolutionary rates and estimating the dates of the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of individual PGs, we found that rates of mutation were similar among PGs (between 6.46 × 10−7 substitutions per site per year [PG1] to 9.54 × 10−7 substitutions per site per year [PG2]).
evidence: This is derived from BEAST analysis of temporal data.

claim: The mutation rate for PG1 is 6.46 × 10−7 substitutions per site per year.
source: Inferring evolutionary rates and estimating the dates of the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of individual PGs, we found that rates of mutation were similar among PGs (between 6.46 × 10−7 substitutions per site per year [PG1] to 9.54 × 10−7 substitutions per site per year [PG2]).
evidence: This is derived from BEAST analysis of temporal data.

claim: The mutation rate for PG2 is 9.54 × 10−7 substitutions per site per year.
source: Inferring evolutionary rates and estimating the dates of the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of individual PGs, we found that rates of mutation were similar among PGs (between 6.46 × 10−7 substitutions per site per year [PG1] to 9.54 × 10−7 substitutions per site per year [PG2]).
evidence: This is derived from BEAST analysis of temporal data.

claim: The mutation rates for S. flexneri are consistent with previous estimates for S. flexneri (3.2 × 10−7 substitutions per site per year).
source: These mutation rates are consistent with previous estimates for S. flexneri (3.2 × 10−7 substitutions per site per year [Zhang et al., 2014]), S. sonnei (6.0 × 10−7 substitutions per site per year [Holt et al., 2012]) and S. dysenteriae (6.52 × 10−7 substitutions per site per year [Rohmer et al., 2014]).
evidence: This claim compares the study results to published literature.

claim: The mutation rate for S. sonnei is 6.0 × 10−7 substitutions per site per year.
source: These mutation rates are consistent with previous estimates for S. flexneri (3.2 × 10−7 substitutions per site per year [Zhang et al., 2014]), S. sonnei (6.0 × 10−7 substitutions per site per year [Holt et al., 2012]) and S. dysenteriae (6.52 × 10−7 substitutions per site per year [Rohmer et al., 2014]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The mutation rate for S. dysenteriae is 6.52 × 10−7 substitutions per site per year.
source: These mutation rates are consistent with previous estimates for S. flexneri (3.2 × 10−7 substitutions per site per year [Zhang et al., 2014]), S. sonnei (6.0 × 10−7 substitutions per site per year [Holt et al., 2012]) and S. dysenteriae (6.52 × 10−7 substitutions per site per year [Rohmer et al., 2014]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The median age of the MRCA for all phylogenetic groups was between 150 and 900 years ago.
source: Using these data we predicted the MRCA of each PG, finding that the median age of the MRCA for all PGs was between 150 and 900 years ago (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplements 4–7).
evidence: This is derived from BEAST temporal analysis shown in Figure 1 and supplements.

claim: PG1, 2, 4 and 6 are the oldest lineages with median BEAST estimates of MRCAs dating to between 1341 and 1659.
source: Of the PGs, PG1, 2, 4 and 6 are the oldest lineages with median BEAST estimate of MRCAs of these groups dating to between 1341 and 1659.
evidence: This is derived from BEAST temporal analysis.

claim: PG5 has a median estimated MRCA dating to 1822.
source: Contrastingly, PG5 and PG3, the latter containing the majority of serotype 2a isolates—one of the key suggested S. flexneri vaccine targets—are much younger, and these PGs have median estimated MRCAs dating to 1822 (PG5) and 1848 (PG3); contemporaneous with the MRCA of the emergence of S. sonnei from Europe.
evidence: This is derived from BEAST temporal analysis.

claim: PG3 has a median estimated MRCA dating to 1848.
source: Contrastingly, PG5 and PG3, the latter containing the majority of serotype 2a isolates—one of the key suggested S. flexneri vaccine targets—are much younger, and these PGs have median estimated MRCAs dating to 1822 (PG5) and 1848 (PG3); contemporaneous with the MRCA of the emergence of S. sonnei from Europe.
evidence: This is derived from BEAST temporal analysis.

claim: PG3 contains the majority of serotype 2a isolates.
source: Contrastingly, PG5 and PG3, the latter containing the majority of serotype 2a isolates—one of the key suggested S. flexneri vaccine targets—are much younger, and these PGs have median estimated MRCAs dating to 1822 (PG5) and 1848 (PG3); contemporaneous with the MRCA of the emergence of S. sonnei from Europe.
evidence: This is shown in the phylogenetic tree and serotype distribution in Figure 1.

claim: The emergence of new S. flexneri PGs did not result in displacement or replacement of isolates from other PGs.
source: However, unlike S. sonnei, the emergence of new S. flexneri PGs did not appear to result in displacement or replacement of isolates from other PGs; rather the older PGs have persisted and continue to cause disease alongside the newer PGs, as evidenced by the fact that every PG contains at least one strain collected since 2008 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal distribution of isolates across PGs.

claim: Every phylogenetic group contains at least one strain collected since 2008.
source: However, unlike S. sonnei, the emergence of new S. flexneri PGs did not appear to result in displacement or replacement of isolates from other PGs; rather the older PGs have persisted and continue to cause disease alongside the newer PGs, as evidenced by the fact that every PG contains at least one strain collected since 2008 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is documented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Regions where S. flexneri is endemic simultaneously support at least two populations of S. flexneri originating from distinct PGs.
source: We observed considerable genomic diversity in S. flexneri isolates collected from the same region. Regions where S. flexneri is endemic simultaneously supported at least two populations of S. flexneri originating from distinct PGs; with the Indian subcontinent having geographically-monophyletic sublineages from four different PGs (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplements 4–6, Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the phylogeographic analysis shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The Indian subcontinent has geographically-monophyletic sublineages from four different phylogenetic groups.
source: We observed considerable genomic diversity in S. flexneri isolates collected from the same region. Regions where S. flexneri is endemic simultaneously supported at least two populations of S. flexneri originating from distinct PGs; with the Indian subcontinent having geographically-monophyletic sublineages from four different PGs (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplements 4–6, Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the phylogeographic analysis shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Most geographically monophyletic sublineages within the PGs had MRCAs in the range of 25–150 years.
source: None of these sublineages are recently introduced into these regions; most geographically monophyletic sublineages within the PGs had MRCAs in the range of 25–150 years.
evidence: This is derived from BEAST temporal analysis.

claim: PG2 has a MRCA dated to 1550 (95% CI: 1340–1725).
source: For example, PG2 has a MRCA dated to 1550 (95% CI: 1340–1725), with Asian isolates appearing in both sublineages of this cluster (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is derived from BEAST temporal analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The MRCA for Asian isolates in PG2 was estimated to be 1544.
source: The MRCA for the Asian isolates was estimated to be 1544; however the African isolates form a single cluster that has a more recent MRCA—dated to 1885 (95% CI: 1833–1923); a result that implies that PG2 S. flexneri was likely introduced into Africa from Asia at least 130 years ago.
evidence: This is derived from BEAST temporal analysis.

claim: The MRCA for African isolates in PG2 was dated to 1885 (95% CI: 1833–1923).
source: The MRCA for the Asian isolates was estimated to be 1544; however the African isolates form a single cluster that has a more recent MRCA—dated to 1885 (95% CI: 1833–1923); a result that implies that PG2 S. flexneri was likely introduced into Africa from Asia at least 130 years ago.
evidence: This is derived from BEAST temporal analysis.

claim: PG2 S. flexneri was likely introduced into Africa from Asia at least 130 years ago.
source: The MRCA for the Asian isolates was estimated to be 1544; however the African isolates form a single cluster that has a more recent MRCA—dated to 1885 (95% CI: 1833–1923); a result that implies that PG2 S. flexneri was likely introduced into Africa from Asia at least 130 years ago.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogeographic and temporal analysis.

claim: There is very limited evidence of large-scale species-wide recombination within the S. flexneri genome.
source: Perhaps surprisingly for a gastrointestinal pathogen of the E. coli complex, at least on a population level, we found very limited evidence of large-scale species-wide recombination within the genome (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), with S. flexneri displaying a recombination profile more in line with the lifestyle-restricted ST131 than with members of other gastrointestinal pathovars such as ETEC (McNally et al., 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the recombination analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: S. flexneri displays a recombination profile more in line with lifestyle-restricted ST131 than with ETEC.
source: Perhaps surprisingly for a gastrointestinal pathogen of the E. coli complex, at least on a population level, we found very limited evidence of large-scale species-wide recombination within the genome (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), with S. flexneri displaying a recombination profile more in line with the lifestyle-restricted ST131 than with members of other gastrointestinal pathovars such as ETEC (McNally et al., 2013).
evidence: This comparison is made based on the recombination analysis and cited literature.

claim: Where recombination could be identified in the virulence repertoire, it was generally present among all isolates within a single PG(s), indicating ancestral recombination prior to PG divergence.
source: Within the virulence repertoire, where recombination could be identified, it was generally present among all isolates within a single PG(s), indicating that the recombination was likely to be ancestral occurring prior to PG divergence.
evidence: This is inferred from the recombination patterns observed in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most evident recombination is restricted to previously identified mobile genetic elements.
source: Furthermore, most evident recombination is restricted to previously identified mobile genetic elements (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the recombination analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Many known virulence functions are ubiquitous to all phylogenetic groups.
source: By examining known chromosomally encoded virulence determinants, it is clear that many known virulence functions are ubiquitous to all PGs (Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the virulence gene distribution shown in Figure 2.

claim: The virulence plasmid and aerobactin were acquired early in S. flexneri evolutionary history and have been subsequently retained.
source: The distribution of virulence determinants indicated that many of the genes/islands whose loss is known to attenuate S. flexneri virulence (such as the VP [Sansonetti et al., 1982] and aerobactin [Lawlor et al., 1987; Wyckoff et al., 2009]) were acquired early in its evolutionary history and have been subsequently retained.
evidence: This is inferred from the virulence gene distribution shown in Figure 2 and supported by citations.

claim: Sat (Serine Protease Autotransporter) is found in PGs 2, 4, and 7, but absent from PGs 1, 3, 5 or 6.
source: However, some variation in the composition of virulence determinants is also evident. For example, Sat, a Serine Protease Autotransporter, is found in PGs 2, 4, and 7, but absent from PGs 1, 3, 5 or 6 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the virulence gene distribution shown in Figure 2.

claim: PGs 1, 3, 5 and 6 possess a genetic scar suggesting that Sat was present ancestrally and has been subsequently lost.
source: For example, Sat, a Serine Protease Autotransporter, is found in PGs 2, 4, and 7, but absent from PGs 1, 3, 5 or 6 (Figure 2). Although the latter PGs possess a genetic scar suggesting that Sat was present ancestrally and has been subsequently lost.
evidence: This is inferred from genomic analysis.

claim: The SHI-1 pathogenicity island was acquired once between 1848 and 1882 near the root of PG3.
source: We also find that the SHI-1 pathogenicity island—a distinguishing feature of serotype 2a (the dominant serotype causing disease world-wide [Kotloff et al., 1999])—was acquired once (between 1848 and 1882) near to the root of PG3.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution and temporal analysis.

claim: SHI-1 carries genes encoding three key virulence associated proteins: Pic, SigA, and ShET1.
source: SHI-1 carries genes encoding three key virulence associated proteins—Pic, (Henderson et al., 1999) SigA (Al-Hasani et al., 2000), and the S. flexneri enterotoxin ShET1 (Fasano et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Pic encodes a secreted protease that has mucinase activity and has been suggested to be involved in haemagglutination and serum resistance.
source: Pic, which is also found in Enteroaggregative E. coli, encodes a secreted protease that has been shown to have mucinase activity and has been suggested to be involved in haemagglutination and serum resistance (Henderson et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: SigA is thought to be involved in fluid accumulation.
source: SigA is thought to be involved in fluid accumulation (Al-Hasani et al., 2000), while the S. flexneri enterotoxin ShET1 has also been shown to be involved in fluid accumulation in rabbit ileal loop models (Fasano et al., 1997), and has been proposed as being the causative agent of the voluminous watery diarrhoea characteristic of a S. flexneri serotype 2a infection (Noriega et al., 1995; Fasano et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: ShET1 has been shown to be involved in fluid accumulation in rabbit ileal loop models.
source: SigA is thought to be involved in fluid accumulation (Al-Hasani et al., 2000), while the S. flexneri enterotoxin ShET1 has also been shown to be involved in fluid accumulation in rabbit ileal loop models (Fasano et al., 1997), and has been proposed as being the causative agent of the voluminous watery diarrhoea characteristic of a S. flexneri serotype 2a infection (Noriega et al., 1995; Fasano et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: ShET1 has been proposed as the causative agent of the voluminous watery diarrhoea characteristic of S. flexneri serotype 2a infection.
source: SigA is thought to be involved in fluid accumulation (Al-Hasani et al., 2000), while the S. flexneri enterotoxin ShET1 has also been shown to be involved in fluid accumulation in rabbit ileal loop models (Fasano et al., 1997), and has been proposed as being the causative agent of the voluminous watery diarrhoea characteristic of a S. flexneri serotype 2a infection (Noriega et al., 1995; Fasano et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: SHI-1 is present in 135 of 146 PG3 isolates.
source: Although SHI-1 is only present in PG3 (135 of 146 PG3 isolates included carried this island), it is present in the range of serotypes found within this phylogroup—including multiple isolates of serotypes 1a, 2a, 2b and 5a.
evidence: This is derived from the virulence gene screening shown in Figure 2.

claim: SHI-1 is present in multiple serotypes within PG3, including serotypes 1a, 2a, 2b and 5a.
source: Although SHI-1 is only present in PG3 (135 of 146 PG3 isolates included carried this island), it is present in the range of serotypes found within this phylogroup—including multiple isolates of serotypes 1a, 2a, 2b and 5a.
evidence: This is derived from the virulence gene screening and serotype data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The SHI-1 toxin is not peculiar to strains carrying a particular serotype, but rather to strains within PG3 that are predominantly serotype 2a.
source: This demonstrates that the toxin is not peculiar to strains carrying a particular serotype, but rather to strains within a PG that are predominantly serotype 2a; consistent with reports of a small number of non-2a serotypes reported to encode this toxin (Noriega et al., 1995).
evidence: This is inferred from the distribution of SHI-1 across serotypes within PG3 and supported by citation.

claim: There is evidence for recombination amongst the genes responsible for serotype.
source: More generally, we observe evidence for recombination amongst the genes responsible for serotype (see gtr Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which remains the de-facto method for describing strains of Shigella.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the recombination analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no significant difference between classical and in silico molecular serotyping schemes.
source: When cross comparing the classical and in silico molecular serotyping schemes (Sun et al., 2011) we saw no significant difference in the serotypes predicted (assessed using a Kolmogorov–Smirnov test).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of serotyping methods.

claim: All phylogenetic groups contained multiple serotypes.
source: However, our results do demonstrate that while certain serotypes make up the majority of certain clusters (Figure 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), all of the PGs contained multiple serotypes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the serotype distribution shown in Figure 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Serotype switching occurs in S. flexneri, undermining the principle that serotype can be used as a basis for describing lineage properties or for epidemiological surveillance.
source: This indicates that although the core genome is remarkably stable, serotype switching does occur undermining the principle that serotype can be used either as a basis for describing the properties of a lineage or for epidemiological surveillance and tracking.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of multiple serotypes within phylogenetic groups.

claim: Vaccines targeting a particular backbone using a serotype could be susceptible to the effects of serotype switching.
source: These results also imply that vaccines targeting a particular backbone using a serotype (such as a 2a vaccine to target SHI-1 encoding isolates from PG3) could be susceptible to the effects of serotype switching.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of serotype switching within phylogenetic groups.

claim: The sit locus has been sporadically lost across the S. flexneri tree.
source: In addition to our observations around SHI-1 and the VP we also observed some variation in virulence factor complement within PGs principally for Iron uptake functions; the sit (Runyen-Janecky et al., 2003) and fec loci (Luck et al., 2001) and enterobactin biosynthesis operon. Across our S. flexneri tree it is apparent that these have contrasting patterns of gain and loss; sit is ancestral, but was sporadically lost (unexpectedly, as it has been reported to be in all clinical isolates previously [Runyen-Janecky et al., 2003]), while fec has been gained sporadically by isolates within PG3, as well as being gained (and retained) on separate occasions by isolates in PG1, 2 and 6.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the virulence gene distribution shown in Figure 2 and contrasts with published literature.

claim: The fec locus has been gained sporadically by isolates within PG3, as well as being gained and retained on separate occasions by isolates in PG1, 2 and 6.
source: Across our S. flexneri tree it is apparent that these have contrasting patterns of gain and loss; sit is ancestral, but was sporadically lost (unexpectedly, as it has been reported to be in all clinical isolates previously [Runyen-Janecky et al., 2003]), while fec has been gained sporadically by isolates within PG3, as well as being gained (and retained) on separate occasions by isolates in PG1, 2 and 6.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the virulence gene distribution shown in Figure 2.

claim: The enterobactin genes are present across PGs 3, 5, 7 and 4, as well as a subset of related isolates within PG1.
source: Of additional interest is the enterobactin operon; which encodes a high affinity iron siderophore (O'Brien and Gibson, 1970). It has previously been reported that in S. flexneri the enterobactin genes are 'rarely utilized' (Schmitt and Payne, 1988; Wyckoff et al., 2009; Reuter et al., 2014); however, our data show that the enterobactin genes are present across PGs 3, 5, 7 and 4, as well as a subset of related isolates within of PG1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the virulence gene distribution shown in Figure 2.

claim: The enterobactin gene phylogenetic topology is the same as that observed for the whole genome tree.
source: Examining the enterobactin gene specifically, we observed the same phylogenetic topology as that observed for the whole genome tree (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2); suggesting this element is ancestral, and has been lost by a subset of PGs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the enterobactin gene phylogeny shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The enterobactin genes are ancestral and have been lost by a subset of phylogenetic groups.
source: Examining the enterobactin gene specifically, we observed the same phylogenetic topology as that observed for the whole genome tree (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2); suggesting this element is ancestral, and has been lost by a subset of PGs.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic analysis of enterobactin genes.

claim: Six tightly clustered isolates within PG3 carry a Shiga toxin 1a (Stx1a)-encoding phage.
source: In addition to these PG-wide patterns, within PG3 we observed six tightly clustered isolates that also carry a Shiga toxin 1a (Stx1a)-encoding phage (Figure 2) which is identical to the recently reported φPOC-J13 (accession number KJ603229) (Gray et al., 2014).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the virulence gene distribution shown in Figure 2.

claim: The Stx1a-encoding phage is identical to the recently reported φPOC-J13.
source: In addition to these PG-wide patterns, within PG3 we observed six tightly clustered isolates that also carry a Shiga toxin 1a (Stx1a)-encoding phage (Figure 2) which is identical to the recently reported φPOC-J13 (accession number KJ603229) (Gray et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The Stx1a-carrying isolates were collected between 2003 and 2008 from Latin America (Haiti, French Guiana and the Dominican Republic).
source: These isolates were collected between 2003 and 2008 from Latin America (Haiti, French Guiana and the Dominican Republic).
evidence: This is documented in the sample metadata.

claim: The Stx1a phage was likely acquired once in this sublineage of PG3.
source: Given that the reference phage clusters phylogenetically within our sequenced isolates it is likely that the phage was acquired once in this sublineage of PG3.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic clustering of Stx1a-carrying isolates.

claim: The Stx1a phage could have been acquired no later than 1998.
source: The dating analysis on the Stx-1-containing PG3 sublineage showed that the phage could have been acquired no later than 1998 (Figure 1—figure supplement 6) suggesting that strains carrying this phage may have been present but undetected in the population for 5–10 years before the earliest reported isolation of Stx1a-producing S. flexneri.
evidence: This is derived from BEAST temporal analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: Strains carrying the Stx1a phage may have been present but undetected in the population for 5–10 years before the earliest reported isolation.
source: The dating analysis on the Stx-1-containing PG3 sublineage showed that the phage could have been acquired no later than 1998 (Figure 1—figure supplement 6) suggesting that strains carrying this phage may have been present but undetected in the population for 5–10 years before the earliest reported isolation of Stx1a-producing S. flexneri.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal analysis.

claim: AMR gene distribution is highly variable both within and across phylogenetic groups.
source: Screening for the presence of known AMR genes (Figure 2) we found that AMR gene distribution was highly variable both within and across PGs (Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the AMR gene distribution shown in Figure 2.

claim: There is little evidence that acquisition of AMR-related loci is linked to the establishment or replacement of dominant lineages in any geographic location.
source: Unlike S. sonnei, we observe little evidence that the acquisition of AMR-related loci is linked to the establishment or replacement of dominant lineages in any geographic location.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogeographic and AMR distribution analysis.

claim: There is limited historical evidence of global expansion of S. flexneri as a result of AMR.
source: While published evidence does exist of one major, on-going, clonal outbreak of S. flexneri in high income countries that has been shown to be the result of a combination of specific epidemiological, AMR and behavioural factors within the MSM community (Baker et al., 2015), examining our dataset focused around historical isolates and those with an origin in low-income countries, we observe limited historical evidence of global expansion as a result of AMR.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogeographic and AMR distribution analysis of the dataset.

claim: The widespread acquisition of AMR determinants occurred independently across the S. flexneri phylogenetic tree.
source: In contrast we observe the widespread acquisition of AMR determinants independently across the tree.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the AMR gene distribution shown in Figure 2.

claim: The SRL-PAI has been introduced independently on at least nine occasions.
source: Our analysis suggests that the SRL-PAI has been introduced independently on at least nine occasions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ancestral state reconstruction shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The SRL-PAI has been maintained in subsequent lineages for protracted periods of time in six cases.
source: In six of these it has been maintained in subsequent lineages for protracted periods of time.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of SRL-PAI shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: There is no evidence of isolates carrying SRL-PAI spreading outside of their geographic region.
source: There is, however, no evidence of isolates carrying SRL-PAI spreading outside of their geographic region, and, once acquired, in a number of cases it appears that the SRL-MDRE may have been subsequently lost (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogeographic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: In a number of cases the SRL-MDRE may have been subsequently lost after acquisition.
source: There is, however, no evidence of isolates carrying SRL-PAI spreading outside of their geographic region, and, once acquired, in a number of cases it appears that the SRL-MDRE may have been subsequently lost (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: There are 23 internal branches where non SRL-PAI resistance determinants have been acquired.
source: Beyond the SRL-PAI we observe 23 internal branches where non SRL-PAI resistance determinants have been acquired (Figure 2), depicting a distinctive wave-like pattern of resistance determinant acquisition over time (Figure 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the AMR gene distribution shown in Figure 2.

claim: The earliest resistance genes observed in the population code for sulphonamide resistance (1950s).
source: The earliest resistance genes observed in the population code for sulphonamide resistance (1950s), followed by streptomycin and tetracycline (1960s) resistance, with β lactamases arising first in strains isolated in the 1970s (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the temporal distribution of AMR genes shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Streptomycin and tetracycline resistance genes appeared in the 1960s.
source: The earliest resistance genes observed in the population code for sulphonamide resistance (1950s), followed by streptomycin and tetracycline (1960s) resistance, with β lactamases arising first in strains isolated in the 1970s (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the temporal distribution of AMR genes shown in Figure 3A.

claim: β-lactamases arose first in strains isolated in the 1970s.
source: The earliest resistance genes observed in the population code for sulphonamide resistance (1950s), followed by streptomycin and tetracycline (1960s) resistance, with β lactamases arising first in strains isolated in the 1970s (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the temporal distribution of AMR genes shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Strains acquiring AMR determinants remain geographically restricted.
source: Notably, we observe that in all cases within S. flexneri the strains acquiring AMR determinants remain geographically restricted, although on a population level we also observe an upward trend in AMR determinant possession over time, in all PGs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogeographic and AMR distribution analysis.

claim: There is an upward trend in AMR determinant possession over time in all phylogenetic groups.
source: Notably, we observe that in all cases within S. flexneri the strains acquiring AMR determinants remain geographically restricted, although on a population level we also observe an upward trend in AMR determinant possession over time, in all PGs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the temporal trend shown in Figure 3B.

claim: S. flexneri strains that do not harbour large numbers of AMR determinants can still be isolated in the 21st century.
source: We also observe that whilst AMR is widespread in the 21st century, we can isolate S. flexneri strains that do not harbour large numbers of AMR determinants; this is in marked contrast to observations within the S. sonnei population.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the AMR distribution shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3.

claim: At a population level, S. flexneri is characterized by long-term colonization of endemic regions with limited evidence of intercontinental transmission within the last 30 years.
source: It is evident from the presented data that, at a population level, S. flexneri is characterised by long-term colonisation of endemic regions, with limited evidence of intercontinental transmission within the last 30 years.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogeographic analysis presented in the results.

claim: Endemic countries support a diverse population of S. flexneri and have done for some time.
source: Our data also suggest that endemic countries support a diverse population of S. flexneri, and have done for some time, implying long-term local-transmission/colonisation in those settings.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic diversity and temporal analysis.

claim: S. sonnei is historically characterized by recent colonization of countries and dominant pandemic lineages with frequent inter-country and inter-continental transmission.
source: This is in direct contrast to S. sonnei, where historically the population is characterised by recent colonisation of countries and dominant pandemic lineages, with frequent inter-country and inter-continental transmission and repeated strain replacement (Holt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: For S. sonnei, acquisition of multiple AMR genes was strongly associated with lineage replacement by dominant resistant lineages on a global scale.
source: For S. sonnei the acquisition of multiple AMR genes was strongly associated with lineage replacement by dominant resistant lineages, on a global scale.
evidence: This is based on comparison with published S. sonnei studies.

claim: For S. flexneri, there have been over 30 independent acquisitions of AMR determinants at a local level with limited global spread.
source: Whereas, for S. flexneri, we observe a population where there have been over 30 independent acquisitions of AMR determinants at a local level; but these acquisitions generally result in limited global spread (Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the AMR distribution and phylogeographic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: AMR may be a significant factor in maintaining existing S. flexneri lineages within specific locales but does not lead to pandemic displacement of other pre-existing lineages.
source: This implies that while AMR may be a significant factor in maintaining existing lineages within specific locales we do not see widespread evidence of AMR acquisition leading to the pandemic displacement of other pre-existing lineages.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogeographic and AMR distribution analysis.

claim: S. flexneri strains can be recovered from the environment in endemic countries unlinked to any outbreak.
source: It has previously been shown that S. flexneri strains can be recovered from the environment in endemic countries (Faruque et al., 2002) unlinked to any outbreak, and that under experimental conditions S. flexneri can survive for several months in water at room temperature (Uyanik et al., 2008), simulated environmental water (Hendricks and Morrison, 1967; Islam et al., 1996) and upon foodstuffs (Islam et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Under experimental conditions S. flexneri can survive for several months in water at room temperature.
source: It has previously been shown that S. flexneri strains can be recovered from the environment in endemic countries (Faruque et al., 2002) unlinked to any outbreak, and that under experimental conditions S. flexneri can survive for several months in water at room temperature (Uyanik et al., 2008), simulated environmental water (Hendricks and Morrison, 1967; Islam et al., 1996) and upon foodstuffs (Islam et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: There are multiple examples of S. flexneri outbreaks where the outbreak strain was traced back to and isolated from local water sources.
source: Furthermore, there are multiple examples of S. flexneri outbreaks where the outbreak strain was traced back to, and isolated from local water sources (Swaddiwudhipong et al., 1995; He et al., 2009; Saha et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Within Bangladesh, S. flexneri disease risk was persistent throughout the year and associated with environmental factors.
source: In addition, at least one study has been undertaken that has demonstrated that within Bangladesh S. flexneri disease risk was persistent throughout the year and associated with environmental factors (geographic location/provision of flood defences) (Emch et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The provision of clean water and good sanitation correlates with a reduction in the rates of S. flexneri disease.
source: When these studies are combined with both our results and additional observations that the provision of clean water and good sanitation correlates with a reduction in the rates of S. flexneri disease (Esrey et al., 1985), we believe that the implication is that in an environment where water is frequently persistently contaminated with faeces, S. flexneri, in effect, persists in the environment, and has been doing so over the long term, in countries around the world.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In environments where water is frequently contaminated with faeces, S. flexneri persists in the environment over the long term.
source: When these studies are combined with both our results and additional observations that the provision of clean water and good sanitation correlates with a reduction in the rates of S. flexneri disease (Esrey et al., 1985), we believe that the implication is that in an environment where water is frequently persistently contaminated with faeces, S. flexneri, in effect, persists in the environment, and has been doing so over the long term, in countries around the world.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of published literature and the study's phylogeographic findings.

claim: The lifecycle of S. flexneri disease is analogous to that of Vibrio cholerae, with part of the pathogen's infectious cycle being in contaminated water.
source: When considering the temporal and phylogeographic analyses presented here in this context, we think that the evidence supports the concept, suggested previously, that in endemic countries the lifecycle of S. flexneri disease is analogous to that of Vibrio cholerae (Faruque et al., 2002); with part of the pathogens infectious cycle being in contaminated water, from which it periodically emerges to cause disease.
evidence: This is inferred from the study's findings and supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The O-antigen carried by Plesiomonas shigelloides is immunologically indistinguishable from the S. sonnei O-antigen.
source: It has been suggested that the O-antigen carried by Plesiomonas shigelloides (another organism isolated from faecally contaminated water)—that is immunologically indistinguishable from the S. sonnei O-antigen may help to explain the contrasting global distribution of S. sonnei and S. flexneri infections (Sack et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Exposure to P. shigelloides through drinking contaminated ground water has been hypothesized to stimulate low level cross protective immunity against S. sonnei.
source: Exposure to P. shigelloides, through drinking contaminated ground water has been hypothesized to stimulate low level cross protective immunity against S. sonnei, explaining why it is rarely found in the resource poor settings but its incidence increases with water sanitation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis discussed in the context of published literature.

claim: S. flexneri is a historic pathogen with a stable core genome equipped with a repertoire of virulence determinants that have enabled it to colonize and persist in multiple locations for hundreds of years.
source: Collectively, our analyses outline a historic pathogen with a stable core genome that comes equipped with a repertoire of virulence determinants that have enabled it to colonise, and persist, in multiple locations for hundreds of years.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic, temporal, and virulence gene analyses presented in the study.

claim: Temporal analysis reveals limited evidence of intercontinental transmission and local colonization of S. flexneri within the last 30 years.
source: However, this life-cycle is at odds with current patterns of human development; with temporal analysis revealing limited evidence of intercontinental transmission and local colonisation within the last 30 years.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogeographic and temporal analyses.

claim: Over the course of the 20th Century, many countries have industrialized with increasing provision of clean water and sanitation possibly disrupting the traditional transmission route of S. flexneri.
source: It may be that this change is reflective of the fact that over the course of the 20th Century, many countries have industrialised; with increasing provision of clean water and sanitation possibly disrupting the traditional transmission route of S. flexneri.
evidence: This is speculated based on the temporal patterns observed and general knowledge of public health improvements.

claim: S. flexneri continues to be a source of disease infecting millions in low-income nations.
source: However, despite its decline in industrialised countries, where transmission of this pathogen by faecally contaminated food and water is well controlled, S. flexneri continues, as it has done for hundreds of years, to be a source of disease infecting millions in the low-income nations of the world.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and the study's findings.
